item.content:encoded:
The "dopamine decor" interiors trend is taking social media by storm, but it's just another disingenuous dressing-up of superficial style as life-improving experience, writes Julie Lasky.

For some time now, the internet has labeled a maximalist decorating trend that embraces candy colors, fuzzy textures and whimsical furnishings "dopamine decor". The reference is, of course, to neuroscience, and supporters claim that the style, which, like many interiors ideas, has its roots in fashion, produces a genuine emotional uplift.

The look is energetic and often charming. Seen on social media, it leaves a stubborn pink glow in the mind as one moves on to a cake-fail video.

For every white-paint-loving minimalist, there has always been a Barbie with a hot-pink dream house

Books celebrate it, too. In April, Rachel Varney, who has an Instagram called The Shoestring Home, published Dopamine Home (Mobius). The publicist described it as "the ultimate mood-boosting guide filled with color know how, creative hacks and cost saving tips and tricks". The central image on the bubblegum-pink cover is of a squiggle-based glass coffee table supporting a ceramic fruit bowl shaped like a bunch of bananas.

And now, Maitri Mody, a New York-based designer whose Instagram is called Honey I Dressed the Pug, is coming out in late August with Dopamine Design: Creating a Home That Makes You Happy (Ten Speed Press). Her goal is to teach readers that they are not chained to conformity but can break away and pursue their own idiosyncratic, ecstatic visions.

"For years, design trends worshiped minimalism," Mody writes, in prose that has the rhythmic cadences and offbeat assertions associated with generative AI. (A detection tool backed me up on that suspicion, though Mody denies using AI to write the book.)

Read:

"True trends always answer a need"

"White walls, neutral furniture, and barely-there decor dominated Instagram feeds and Pinterest boards. But let's be honest – minimalism isn't for everyone. It's a look, not a feeling. Dopamine design flips the script. It's not about following rules or trends. It's about creating a home that celebrates your quirks, your story, and your joy."

Let me pause here to raise an eyebrow at the description of minimalism as "a look, not a feeling". Even its haters describe it as cold, which is most certainly a feeling.

I also object to the use of the color white as a straw man. For every white-paint-loving minimalist like, say, John Pawson, there has always been a Barbie with a hot-pink dream house.

Dopamine decor is said to have influenced the look of food packaging in real life

Let me add that I met Mody in person a few years ago, while she was exhibiting a checkerboard-patterned kitchen with cabinet pulls that looked like carrots, and found her very nice. It is not my intention to whimsy-shame anyone. But given the commoditization of health in everything from peptides to bathing culture, I find it icky to glibly invoke brain chemistry in the marketing of style.

Dopamine decor claims to celebrate individuality, though it's driven by repetitive social media images. It is aimed at adults, though its tutti-frutti, cutesy-naive examples look incontrovertibly juvenile.

It purports to stimulate happy brain chemicals, at a time when, in the US, public health movements are being eviscerated by deranged officials. "'Dopamine decor' can boost your mood," the Washington Post declared last year, like a snake-oil salesman. Well, so can a bucket of tiramisu, until the sugar high lets you down.

Read:

"What to do with the TV is among the most challenging design problems in today's American home"

The most disingenuous thing about this trend is the pretense that images on a screen or in a book represent plausible experience. The photos are filtered, cropped and disjointed. They whiz by, just like an endorphin rush. Dopamine decor is said to have influenced the look of food packaging in real life, but food packages are quickly thrown away.

What are the long-term effects of living with frenetic decorating choices? Do they lose their happy juice over time? Do they get on one's nerves? Do they drive one insane?

Yes, said Ashley Couto, who wrote an article for Business Insider magazine last year with the headline: "I redid my space with color and 'dopamine decor' designed to bring me joy. It worked at first, but I already hate it."

A style touted as authentic and livable can't seem to shed its performative, Instagram-y nature

This would not surprise Andréa de Paiva, a Brazilian architect who specializes in the relationship between neuroscience and building design. In a cautionary article about dopamine decor on the website of her organization, NeuroAU, she writes: "Instead of thoughtfully enhancing the environment to support well-being, these spaces risk overwhelming the senses, potentially leading to fatigue, distraction, or even stress rather than joy and motivation."

De Paiva urges designers to be responsible with terminology, especially when it comes to applied science: "Titles like Dopamine Design or even NeuroArchitecture can be intriguing and marketable, but they should not be used as buzzwords to sell incomplete or oversimplified ideas."

Still, you don't need to be a brain surgeon to recognize that a style touted as authentic and livable can't seem to shed its performative, Instagram-y nature. According to Marianne Plaisance, a graphic designer and photographer featured in Modi's book, some of her YouTube followers thought her space looked AI-generated.

She took it as a compliment.

Julie Lasky is New York-based a journalist and critic specialising in design, architecture and urbanism. She was previously deputy editor of The New York Times' weekly Home and Garden section, the editor of Change Observer, editor-in-chief of ID magazine and editor of Interiors magazine. She is also a part-time assistant professor at Parsons School of Design.

item.content:encoded:
Architecture studios Waugh Thistleton Architects and Mithun have designed a 12-storey mass-timber office block in Bellevue, Washington.

Designed for developer and contractor Skanska, the Bevel tower will become the tallest timber office building in the USA, when it completes. It is also Waugh Thistleton Architects' first project in the US.

"Bevel will be our first built project in the US, but more importantly with a building of this scale it demonstrates that timber is ready to take its place at the forefront of American architecture," said Waugh Thistleton Architects co-founder Andrew Waugh.

The 55-metre-high office block will have a hybrid timber and steel structure with mass-timber columns, beams and ceilings exposed throughout the building.

According to US timber advocacy organisation WoodWorks, the building will be the tallest mass-timber office building in the US.

"Bevel is notable for what will become the tallest mass-timber office building in the US, but it's also expanding the idea of what's possible with these projects," said WoodWorks CEO Jennifer Cover.

"Of the 22 tall timber buildings under construction or built, only three are commercial. A tremendous amount of work also went into gaining approval for the 100 per cent exposed timber ceilings. In both areas, Bevel is setting an example that advances the options available to other building designers."

Read:

Dalston Works demonstrated that "timber is a viable alternative to concrete and steel at scale"

The structure will have a concrete foundation and car park in its base with a timber structure above ground. This will be supported by a steel core and seismic supports.

According to Mithun, the timber structure made it possible to design more appealing floor plans than a concrete equivalent.

"Early in the project, our team evaluated mass timber alongside a concrete construction option," said Mithun partner Craig Curtis.

"For this tight site, a standard concrete approach with a centralised core created narrow office floor plates and limited connectivity across the rentable area," he continued.

"By contrast, the mass timber scheme supports a side core and more open floor plates, creating a stronger leasing proposition and unique work environment. In this study, mass timber also achieved cost parity with concrete due in part to efficient timber design and decreased construction schedule planning"

Waugh Thistleton Architects has designed numerous timber buildings, including the first mass-timber skyscrapers and the world's largest cross-laminated timber building.

item.content:encoded:
French-German designer Tatjana von Stein designed hundreds of bespoke lights and furnishings for this hotel in Munich, drawing on the city's art nouveau style and its exuberant nightlife history.

The Dean Munich is the latest offering from the Irish hotel chain, with 281 rooms and suites, three bars, and a signature Japanese restaurant named Ibasho.

The project saw von Stein revamp an existing hotel in the city's Westend neighbourhood, with a design where shades of gold and red extend across velvet furniture, floral carpets, stained-glass windows and ornamental lamps.

The project allowed the interior designer to dig into the design history of the city where she was born. Her scheme blends the city's distinct Jugendstil style, the manifestation of art nouveau in Bavaria, with the decadent nightclubs that proliferated in the 1980s.

"This is a city rooted in history but always drawn to reinvention," said von Stein. "I wanted to capture that tension, somewhere between elegance and exuberance, and let it guide every surface, object and gesture."

"The design also brings to life a side of Munich only locals truly know – its rich musical and cultural spirit, quietly woven into the character of the city."

The most radical interventions are in the communal areas on the ground floor, which were completely reorganised.

They begin with the lobby, a space with a rich sense of theatricality. At its centre is a stepped platform, where a wrap-around bar is set below a circular ceiling recess with a reflective surface and a decorative wallpaper frieze around its edges.

This is the first of many playful ceilings that feature throughout the hotel.

On either side of the bar, lounge areas are framed by tiered ceiling recesses with zigzagging corners, matching the edge details of the internal columns.

Read:

Traditional wooden townhouses inform interiors of Kengo Kuma-designed Capella Kyoto hotel

"We're really interior architects, so we start with layout and hard finishes before slowly making our way into furniture and fixtures," von Stein told Dezeen.

"I love to fully envelop people in a world, and that starts with the envelope. So ceilings certainly play a big part."

Over the restored chevron-tiled stone flooring, the rest of the space is carefully layered with patterned rugs and gloss-backed sofas, while focal points include bell-shaped sconces, frilled stools and sculptural tables.

Many of the objects here were custom-designed by von Stein, although she also sourced some vintage pieces, including original late-19th and early-20th century pieces by Austrian design icons Josef Hoffmann and Otto Wagner.

She points to a pair of sphinx table lights as a personal favourite in this room, "somehow out of place, but fabulous".

Japanese influences come into play in Ibasho, inspired by the cuisine of chef Alex Craciun.

Below mirrored and fluted ceilings, von Stein created a series of "rooms within rooms". These include a conversation pit with gold velvet sofas and a horseshoe-shaped marble bar encircled by pink leather Verner Panton chairs.

The Jugendstil-inspired stained glass frames a series of windows between these spaces, offering glimpsed views between them.

"For me, the most compelling hospitality spaces are those that reveal themselves gradually," said von Stein.

"We wanted to create a space which engages the senses, influences mood and encourages a certain rhythm of experience and connection throughout the diner's experience."

Tucked away behind Ibasho, Noren is a more exclusive and intimate cocktail bar. This 48-seat space features Friendly Pressure speakers, a geometric timber ceiling and tapestry-style seating.

The style is more pared-back in the bedrooms, but no less stylish. Against a backdrop of panelled walls, olive-green and orange textiles sit alongside tubular shelving units, tiger-stripe tables and sculptural chairs.

As with the communal areas, these rooms are embellished with works by Munich-based contemporary artists. These were curated by Christian Ganzenberg, the director of Munich's international art festival, Various Others.

For The Dean, the hotel is its largest to date and its second outside Ireland, following the Berlin hotel designed by Rachael Gowdridge, showcased on Dezeen earlier this year.

It also marks the latest in a series of lavish hospitality spaces designed by von Stein, following members' club Làlia in Palma, Mallorca, and the Locke am Platz hotel in Zurich, Switzerland.

In a recent interview with Dezeen, the designer described her approach as both theatrical and precise.

"Let's face it, the world is rather chaotic and can be quite a depressing place," she told Dezeen's deputy editor, Cajsa Carlson. "So these moments of theatre are important, and decadence to a certain extent."

The photography is by Dean Hearne, courtesy of The Dean.

item.content:encoded:
Dutch studio Woonpioniers has completed CoHouse in Utrecht, a pair of interlocking houses designed for two families within a single gabled volume.

Amsterdam-based Woonpioniers was tasked with creating adjoining yet distinct residences for the two families, who had bought a verdant riverside plot in the village of Cothen to build homes but were required by the local municipality to fit them within a single volume.

The result is a 237-square-metre co-housing project comprising two matching-sized dwellings that overlap on their upper floors in a layout described by the studio as "a game of Tetris".

"Two families chose to build together, but the municipality required both homes to fit within a single building volume," studio partner Leen Bogerd told Dezeen.

"We addressed this by interlocking two equivalent, though distinct, homes," he explained.

"To make the most of the garden, views, privacy and sunlight, the two homes were carefully rotated around each other like a game of Tetris."

Each of the homes was tailored to the needs of the families, with floor plans oriented to overlook an enclosed garden from one residence and the surrounding landscape from another.

According to Woonpioniers, both families requested a low-carbon approach to the build, resulting in a structural timber frame, cross-laminated timber floors and wood-fibre insulation. A bio-based acoustic build-up was used for the party floor between the homes.

Accounting for the homes' energy demand are ground-source heat pumps, a heat-recovery ventilation system and a solar roof.

Other sustainability strategies used by the studio include external shading on the building's south and west-facing facades, which are finished in timber cladding and render.

Read:

Woonpioniers opts for "modernity tucked inside tradition" at timber-lined Dutch home

"For both the architects and the two families, the central ambition was to create a healthy, ecological and bio-based home with a low environmental impact," he continued.

"This led to a timber-based construction system, while also requiring careful solutions for fire safety and acoustics."

Accessed through a shared entrance area, both homes lead into an open-plan kitchen and dining area at ground level, where large openings have been designed to "soften the boundary between the homes and a shared garden".

In one residence, a double-height void draws daylight into the ground-floor dining area below, beside which an open timber staircase leads up to four bedrooms and a bathroom on the upper floor.

Meanwhile, the second home has a more closed layout, complete with four spacious bedrooms on its upper floor.

Exposed timber surfaces are paired with grey-toned flooring and neutral tones throughout the interiors.

Elsewhere in Utrecht, Woonpioniers also recently completed a timber-lined home within a pair of gabled volumes.

The studio has previously created a prefabricated wooden cabin with large windows and tall, curving interiors within a forest glade in the Netherlands.

With much of the world suffering from heatwaves and the UK set to experience its hottest summer on record, we have collected five ice cream stores that offer a temporary cool fix.

Our love for ice cream is global, as proven by these stylish shops in locations ranging from London to Buenos Aires.

SR Ice Cream Miyakojima, Japan, by Kii

Located on an island in the southern part of Japan's Okinawa prefecture in the Pacific Ocean, SR features local materials including limestone and perforated concrete bricks.

It also has a striking curved pink ceiling, whose colour was chosen to "ensure it harmonised with the environment at any time of day or night," Kii co-founder Satoshi Arai told Dezeen.

Find out more about SR Ice Cream Miyakojima ›

Veneciana Canning Ice Cream Drive Thru, Argentina, by DRM Arquitectura

This striking ice cream store sits on inverted V-columns on a busy roadside plot near National Route No. 58 in Buenos Aires.

Architecture studio DRM Arquitectura built the drive-through store as a "quick-build roadside stop" that would also function as an "announcement sign" for travellers in the area.

Find out more about Veneciana Canning Ice Cream Drive Thru ›

Little Sky, Australia, by Ewert Leaf

Local studio Ewert Leaf designed the Little Sky ice cream shop in Melbourne, Australia, to showcase the gelato-making process.

In its roomy interior, pink and blue hues are juxtaposed with terrazzo tables and solid-oak seats.

Find out more about Little Sky ›

Milk Train, UK, by FormRoom

London's Covent Garden neighbourhood is home to Milk Train, a store designed to "cater primarily to [the brand's] diverse Instagram demographic".

Here, design studio FormRoom created cloud ceilings and neon signage to complement the brand's creative offerings, which include candy floss ice cream.

This small ice cream parlour in the Czech city of Brno is filled with arches and undulating surfaces.

item.content:encoded:
Spanish studio NUA Arquitectures has renovated a textile warehouse near Barcelona, using timber partitions to create a small office block within its concrete-and-brick structure.

The project was completed for Tuvatèxtil, one of the last companies still operating in El Pont d'Armentera – once the most important textile hub in southern Catalonia, home to 12 factories.

With much of this heritage now gone, NUA Arquitectures looked to retain and celebrate the remaining warehouse's existing fabric, inserting a new block of offices housed within a standalone timber structure.

"The project recovers, reclaims, and celebrates the industrial and textile history of El Pont d’Armentera," NUA Arquitectures told Dezeen.

"It is a mediation between memory, identity, and the act of dwelling – adaptive retention and radical reuse," it added.

At the northwestern entrance to the offices, a communal paved plaza has been created, sheltered by a vaulted canopy made of concrete and terracotta-coloured steel, and dotted with trees and curving lampposts.

This leads into a corner of the existing warehouse that has been enclosed with timber and glass partitions, creating the effect of a building-within-a-building that houses two floors of office and meeting spaces.

"The project is conceived from the idea of transition and unfolds around the new tree-lined square – a central node for gathering, resting, and celebration – located at the heart of the factory complex," explained the studio.

To the west, these offices extend beyond the footprint of the existing factory, forming a small single-storey block topped by a band of patterned tiles. This contains a dining area and kitchen that overlook the plaza.

A terracotta-paved route, dubbed the red carpet by the studio, leads from the plaza through the offices. It ends in a staircase and ramp that lead down to the warehouse floor, which is overlooked by a timber-framed balcony above.

Read:

Muhhe Studio inserts "wooden box" into old factory to create light-filled photographer's studio

"The primary working medium is the existing building fabric itself, both physical and contextual," NUA Arquitectures explained.

"Consequently, all viable elements, including stone, are recycled, while lightweight tectonics, such as timber and ceramics, are used for the rehabilitation."

The concrete and brick structure of the surrounding warehouse has been reinforced to allow for the creation of new openings and skylights, while its walls have been updated with external insulation.

NUA Arquitectures was founded in Tarragona in 2013 by Arnau Tiñena, Ferran Tiñena and Maria Rius. Previous projects by the studio include the renovation of an old stone house and the Casa Juià farmhouse, both in Catalonia.

item.content:encoded:
Los Angeles studio Ome Dezin has partnered with design platform Lumens to renovate and furnish a 1990s home in the Hollywood Hills, adding iconic furniture and lighting from Frank Gehry, Ingo Maurer and more.

Situated in middle of a mature forest on over an acre of land, the house was originally designed by architect Jeff Mills in a style that blends mid-century modern and brutalism.

The residence was once home to an A-list actor, then later converted into an art gallery, leaving white-washed walls, tall ceilings, exposed beams and expansive spaces for Ome Dezin founders Jesse Rudolph and Joelle Kutner to build upon.

"It was stripped of all personality," the duo told Dezeen. "There were no doors, bedrooms, full bathrooms, etc. It was hard for some to envision this house as a home."

They restored the original architecture, making minor alterations like adding a gym, converting an upstairs guest bedroom into the primary bathroom and erecting an exterior sauna and full bathroom.

Limestone flooring in some of the rooms was saved, while all the other surfaces were altered or added to in order to transform the property into a livable home.

"The space felt sterile when we got into it, and our goal was to bring depth, layers, and warmth to the home," the pair said.

With the surrounding forested landscape in mind, Rudolph and Kutner used wood to clad entire walls in the main living spaces and bathrooms.

They also introduced atypically tall wood baseboards to create a sense of continuity throughout the home, while stone such as richly veined marble in the bathrooms was also employed to embellish the natural aesthetic.

The kitchen is enveloped in a distinctive blue stone, while the island is clad in a rust-toned variation with an aged, tactile finish.

"Throughout the home, these earthy materials are punctuated by glimmers of jewel tones, silver, and gold — appearing in the lighting, decorative details, and custom stained-glass windows and doors we designed specifically for the space," said the team.

Willett and Ome Dezin renovate mid-century CM G1 House in LA

When it came to furnishing the residence, Ome Dezin teamed up with Lumens – a platform they already used frequently to source furniture and lighting – to choose distinctive pieces to complete the spaces.

They began with lighting, selecting favourites such as gold Ingo Maurer pendants for the kitchen, along with pieces from Foscarini and In Common With.

"Lighting is so important to us as we think of it as functional art," said Rudolph and Kutner. "It adds warmth, character, depth and shadows into a space for layer and movement."

Furniture was then layered in, from Gubi dining chairs to statement pieces like a striped Up chair by Gaetano Pesce and Frank Gehry's Wiggle Chair.

"What I love about the result is that you feel the individuality of each piece, but nothing feels overly coordinated," Lumens chief marketing officer Dana Gers told Dezeen. "There's a sense of discovery to it. It feels collected, personal and entirely at home within the architecture."

As an interior design and development studio, Ome Dezin reimagined, renovated and sold multiple properties across the greater Los Angeles area.

These include a 1960s A Quincy Jones house in Brentwood and a mid-century Laurel Hills residence for which they collaborated with furniture designer Willet.

item.content:encoded:
Local studio Helen & Hard has completed a timber cabin on Norway's Atlantic coast where sprawling tree-like columns made from uprooted spruce trees frame panoramic views of the sea.

Named Cabin Sande, the 112-square-metre retreat on a protected rocky headland in Randaberg occupies the footprint of a 1970s cabin. Planning restrictions required the replacement building to match the original's size and height.

Helen & Hard placed the low, angular building on a stone plinth made from rock found on site and topped it with a planted roof that follows the contours of the surrounding terrain.

The cabin is organised around 18 branching columns made from whole spruce trees, including their root systems.

Each tree was excavated with its roots intact before being cleaned, air-dried for eight months and digitally scanned, allowing robots to mill bespoke joints while preserving the organic shape of each tree.

The spruce columns spread into the ceiling like tree canopies before branching into bookshelves, benches, stairs, room dividers, window frames, doors, the kitchen and the fireplace.

Read:

Helen & Hard hangs Woodnest treehouses from pine trees above Norwegian fjord

"We wanted to evoke the experience of standing beneath a canopy of trees," Helen & Hard told Dezeen.

"As you move through the space, the rhythmic sequence of the timber columns and the organic character of the structure create a strong sense of shelter and protection."

The structural system draws on traditional Norwegian boatbuilding dating back to the Viking Age, where naturally curved joints between tree trunks and roots were used to stiffen the ribs of wooden vessels.

The fan-shaped cabin opens towards the Atlantic Ocean, where a 9.5-metre-wide window stretches across the main living space without any mullions interrupting the view.

Continuous glazing wraps around much of the cabin, bringing changing light, reflections and weather into the interior, while stepped window sills create a greater sense of enclosure away from the sea.

At the opposite end, a narrow entrance faces a sheltered garden, creating a direct sightline through the building from the vegetation behind to the sea beyond.

Two rows of cantilevered timber beams meet above the panoramic window, allowing the roof to project beyond the glazing to shelter it from the weather.

"The weather along the Atlantic coast can be extremely harsh," said the studio.

"The deep roof overhang and the arrangement of the timber structure create a sheltered, intimate place that simultaneously opens toward the sea."

A concealed system of tension cables and springs helps counteract the weight of the overhanging roof, keeping the glazed opening free from supporting columns.

The main living space sits between a kitchen and covered terrace on one side and two workspaces on the other, one raised on a half level above the bathroom.

Side spaces branch off the central room, creating more intimate places to work, cook and relax beneath the timber structure.

Founded in Stavanger in 1996 by Siv Helene Stangeland and Reinhard Kropf, Helen & Hard works across housing, cultural buildings and public projects, with a focus on timber construction and digital fabrication.

Previous projects by the studio include the Woodnest treehouses overlooking Hardangerfjord and the Vindmøllebakken co-housing development in Stavanger.

The photography is by Ivar Kvaal and Sindre Ellingsen.

item.content:encoded:
The electric vehicle market remains dominated by chunky SUVs, but some carmakers are also producing battery-powered hatchbacks that are modest in size but bold in design. Here, we round up six of the most eye-catching.

Car manufacturers continue to favour larger models for electric vehicles (EVs). They argue that the heavy batteries are more suitable for heftier cars, though some experts have also pointed out that profit margins tend to be bigger on SUVs and SUV crossovers.

But particularly in European cities, demand for more compact EVs is on the rise, with some municipalities seeking to restrict so-called "carspreading" via regulation.

As a result, we're seeing a growing group of EV hatchbacks enter the scene. Some brands have chosen simply to make electrified versions of popular combustion-engine cars – such as the Mini Cooper and the Fiat 500 – but others have taken the opportunity to experiment with a new design language.

Below, we've rounded up six production EVs that can still stand out on the street despite relatively diminutive proportions:

Hyundai Ioniq 3

Launched in April and due to go on sale in the UK and Europe later in 2026, the Ioniq 3 is described by Hyundai as an "aero hatch".

The brand says its swooping shape is determined by the natural bending behaviour of sheet steel.

It riffs directly off the Concept Three, unveiled in September 2025. Speaking to Dezeen at a media preview for the concept car, Hyundai Design Center head Simon Loasby said "we're due a renaissance" in small, cool cars.

Hyundai Inster

Also from Hyundai, though not part of its Ioniq electric sub-brand, is the Hyundai Inster. Launched in 2024, the Inster is in fact an updated, electrified version of the combustion-engine Casper, which is only available in South Korea.

The four-seater is Hyundai's smallest EV. Described by Top Gear magazine as "a cheery looker without toppling into cartoonish cuteness", it makes extensive use of the Korean carmaker's favoured pixelated lighting.

Inside, the cabin is unusually colourful, with the option of patterned upholstery.

Renault 5

Hitting showrooms in early 2025, the electric Renault 5 is a modern, battery-powered interpretation of the French carmaker's classic supermini.

It retains the distinctively angled rear hatchback of the original, which Renault produced from 1972 to 1996.

Other references to various versions of its ancestor can be found in the rear lights, the wheel arches, the bonnet vent and the dashboard.

Contemporary design twists include the A-shaped headlights and their four-cornered motif, which is repeated on the foglights and the dashboard vents.

Honda E (discontinued)

The Honda E arguably kicked off the current wave of design-forward small EVs, having been released in March 2020.

Reminiscent of the work of former Apple chief design officer Jony Ive, its emergence generated significant buzz in the car world.

But despite winning a clutch of awards it sold poorly, with reviewers bemoaning a high price point and limited range, and was ultimately discontinued by Honda in January 2024.

Honda Super N

The Honda E's effective replacement, and a reset of the Japanese manufacturer's entire approach to EVs, is the Super N.

Recently going on sale in the UK, it's a slightly sportier version of the N-One E, which launched in Japan in September 2025.

The Super N is pitched as a super-affordable option, and is in the distinctive boxy, compact style of Japan's kei cars.

Notable touches include colourful seats and simulated engine sounds and gears.

Rivian R3

The R3 is a much-hyped upcoming model from California-based EV company Rivian.

It's the only car on this list planned for availability in the US, though with no confirmation yet on when it will appear in showrooms.

Production is contingent on completion of the brand's new factory in Atlanta, Georgia, which is expected to open in 2028.

While definitely small for an American EV, the R3 will be bigger than it looks in photos. Rivian CEO RJ Scaringe has described it as "a crossover meets an SUV, meets a hatch, meets a wagon, meets a bunch of things".

The R3 will retain Rivian's distinctive face, while the brand's chief design officer, Jeff Hammoud, has claimed that its hatchback shape was inspired by 1980s rally cars such as the Audi Quattro and Lancia Delta Integrale.

item.content:encoded:
This week on Dezeen, Elon Musk announced plans to open a semiconductor factory near Houston, Texas, with a floor area of 100 million square feet that will make it the largest building in the world.

The Terafab factory, a joint chip-building venture for Musk's companies Tesla and SpaceX, will cover an area equivalent to more than 1,700 American football fields in Grimes County, if completed.

It would steal the crown from the current largest building by floor area, Russia's 65 million-square-foot (six million-square-metre) AvtoVAZ main assembly building.

In other technology news, Dezeen revealed that companies publishing realistic AI-generated architectural renderings in the European Union without labelling them risk being fined under a new law that came into force earlier this month.

"If it's realistic scenery with people walking around and it is AI generated, it will need to be labelled as AI generated," said Szymon Sieniewicz, a counsel at law firm Addleshaw Goddard.

In the US, California start-up Satyress unveiled a centaur-like robot called Threehalves, complete with a goat-shaped head.

The four-legged machine, called Threehalves, can be equipped with tools including a chainsaw and remote operated to take on demanding jobs that would put humans at risk of harm.

Automotive company Jaguar has shared a first look at the interior of its upcoming Type 01 electric car – the production version of the controversial Type 00 concept unveiled in 2024.

Renders of the interior show a central divider that runs the full length of the car, effectively separating all of the seats.

In architecture news, UK practice Heatherwick Studio has unveiled scaled-back plans for its redevelopment of an elevated waterfront park in Louisville, Kentucky.

The updated design for the Belvedere park extends green spaces across an existing overpass over a six-lane highway, but is much less ambitious than the original undulating design unveiled by the studio last year due to expense and safety concerns.

Projects that turned our readers' heads this week included a crystal-shaped sauna in Sweden, a cedar-wrapped gallery on a secluded Washington island and a mass-timber groundscraper in Auckland that resembles a "continuous ribbon".

item.content:encoded:
Social media platform Instagram has updated its brand identity with elements such as a refreshed, "bolder and simpler" wordmark and updated typographic elements across the platform.

The update was announced this week and is rolling out globally through 2026 and beyond. Designed in-house, the refresh introduces "something to carry us into the future," said technology company Meta, which owns the platform.

The most notable change is the Instagram wordmark, which has remained the same since 2016. It maintains its cursive, with the serifs have been flattened and detached from the neighbouring letter.

The team said the wordmark pays homage to crafted script to reflect the creativity of Instagram.

"Script reflects individuality, so referencing that felt right," said Instagram director of product design Jasmine Probst.

"The new wordmark is bolder and simpler, with touches of unexpectedness. It cues individual expression, a personal voice, both of which have always been core to Instagram".

Other updates include new typography rolled out across the app, with the platform's gradient colours integrated in "subtle" ways. Motion, layout and UI will also be updated as part of the brand refresh.

Read:

The top rebrands of 2025

In a post from the Instagram Design account, the team said it explored "hundreds of directions" before arriving at something "fresh and simple".

Instagram head Adam Mosseri said it was "time for a refresh" in another recent post on the platform.

"The refreshed brand system puts our community's creativity and self-expression front and center," said Meta director of brand design May Hartono.

"It's designed to spark courageous action and give people the confidence to create and show up as themselves, freely and fully."

Other major technology companies have rebranded in recent years, including Amazon and Google.

It follows a more subtle approach to rebranding seen across these mega corporations, where design changes are almost imperceptible. Dezeen recently rounded up five such projects.

Other companies have taken a bolder approach, such as the American eatery Cracker Barrel, which was met with an explosion of internet backlash.

item.content:encoded:
Architecture studio Populous has completed the steep, metal-clad Highmark Stadium in Buffalo, New York for NFL team the Buffalo Bills, with a canopy and advanced snow-melt system.

The new Highmark Stadium replaces a structure of the same name that is located just across the street in Orchard Park, Buffalo. It opened for the season this past weekend for a training event attended by the team and fans.

The design of the stadium, which features an open-air bowl covered slightly by a steel canopy, is intended to enhance noise within the interior and also protect fans from the city's 95 inches of annual snowfall and other inclement weather.

The majority of the exterior is wrapped in grey semi-translucent perforated metal panels, which wrap an inner 360-degree colonnade populated with concessions.

A dark grey brick features at the structure's base, and the Highmark wordmark features on each aspect.

Inside, the stadium seating is steeper than its predecessor and was designed to bring fans closer to the field.

The canopy itself dips downwards along the stadium's side and rises towards the middle. The roof is outfitted with an extensive hydronic snow-melt system, which will help melt and irrigate snowfall to protect the events below.

Read:

Eight record-breaking stadiums from the biggest to the most expensive

Overall, according to the studio, the design was informed by the historic architecture of Buffalo, such as the Rockpile, the city's former outdoor soccer stadium.

Its towering stainless steel buffalo sculptures were created by artist Blessing Hancock.

The stadium took three years to construct.

Upon its recent opening, some fans took issue with obstructed views at their seats, according to reports.

Populous global director and managing director Jonathan Mallie told local outlet the Buffalo News the obstructed views are a result of creating a higher stacked stadium that would bring fans closer to the field.

"You will find some level of obstruction in every stadium in the world," said Mallie.

"The goal was to bring everybody closer to the field and create an upper deck with an incredible proximity and presence within the bowl to help create a next-level experience for Bills Mafia."

Further images are forthcoming.

Dezeen recently explored the future of stadium design in its Future Stadium series, including why stadium architecture is getting more outlandish and what they may look like in decades to come, according to nine architects.

The images are by Tim McManus, courtesy of Populous.
